name: Infantile Epileptic Spasms Syndrome

criteria.description: Presence of epileptic spasms characterized by sudden flexion, extension, or mixed extension–flexion of predominantly proximal and truncal muscles
Electroencephalogram (EEG) showing hypsarrhythmia or modified hypsarrhythmia pattern
Developmental delay or regression concurrent with onset of spasms
Onset typically between 3 and 12 months of age

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Presence of epileptic spasms plus EEG evidence of hypsarrhythmia and developmental delay or regression
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Hypsarrhythmia may be modified or absent in some cases; clinical correlation is essential.

searchTerms: skin with abnormal texture or color

laboratory: Metabolic screening may reveal underlying etiologies (e.g., inborn errors of metabolism)
CSF analysis typically normal but used to exclude infections
imaging: Brain MRI showing cortical malformations, hypoxic-ischemic injury, or structural abnormalities
Possible cerebral atrophy or delayed myelination
other: EEG demonstrating hypsarrhythmia or modified hypsarrhythmia pattern
Response to adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) or vigabatrin therapy may support diagnosis

distinguishingFeatures: Myoclonic seizures without hypsarrhythmia on EEG
Normal development prior to seizure onset
Different seizure types and EEG patterns
Characteristic skin lesions (hypomelanotic macules, facial angiofibromas)
Seizure types may include infantile spasms but with additional systemic features

redFlags: Onset of spasms beyond 12 months of age
Absence of hypsarrhythmia on EEG despite clinical spasms
Rapid developmental regression or failure to thrive
references: Lux AL, Osborne JP. Infantile spasms: a review of the literature and practical guide to diagnosis and treatment. Eur J Paediatr Neurol. 2004.
Orphanet: Infantile epileptic spasms syndrome. ORPHA:697160.
Shinnar S, et al. Infantile spasms: epidemiology and etiologic classification. Epilepsia. 1997.
